readerTitle: Your real competitor is a spreadsheet
caseNote: 가상 사례 (소규모 운송회사용 배차 앱, 식품 공장용 팔레트 랩핑 기계) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 고객은 우리 제품을 0이나 경쟁사와 비교하지 않는다. 우리가 없을 때 실제로 할 일, 즉 차선책과 비교한다.
misconception: 우리의 경쟁자는 같은 종류의 제품을 파는 회사다. 고객이 지금 아무것도 사지 않고 있다면 경쟁자가 없는 것이다.

sources.text: Fisher, R. & Ury, W. (1981). Getting to Yes. 협상 이론의 BATNA(Best Alternative to a Negotiated Agreement) 개념
마케팅·가격 전략의 표준 개념 (차선책 대비 고객 가치, economic value to the customer)

factChecks.note: 배차 앱 계산: 주 4시간 절약 × 52주 ÷ 12개월 = 월 약 17.3시간(카드에는 약 17시간). 17.3시간 × 시간당 $30 = 약 $520. $520 − 구독료 $200 = $320. 시간당 $30과 주 4시간 절약은 모두 가상 가정입니다.
BATNA라는 용어가 Fisher & Ury의 Getting to Yes(1981)에서 처음 널리 쓰였다는 점을 게시 전에 다시 확인하세요. 카드에는 출처 책 이름과 연도만 적었습니다.
다음 레슨(CUS-02-06 전환 비용)과 겹치지 않도록, 이 레슨은 '무엇과 비교되는가'만 다루고 '바꾸는 데 드는 비용'은 Watch out 카드에서 한 줄로만 예고했습니다.

cards.title: Your real competitor is a spreadsheet
body: A founder builds a dispatch app for small trucking firms. The demo goes well. The owner nods, asks good questions, then says: "We'll stick with what we have."
What they have is a shared spreadsheet, a whiteboard and a dispatcher named Rosa who knows every route by heart. It costs nothing. And it just won the deal.

image.label: Your rival is the workaround they already use.
image.brief: 작은 운송회사 사무실. 화이트보드에 손으로 쓴 배차표, 노트북 화면에 색칠된 스프레드시트, 전화기를 어깨에 낀 배차 담당자. 한쪽 구석에 반쯤 닫힌 세련된 앱 데모 화면. 실제 소프트웨어 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: What should you compare your app against?
body: You sell that dispatch app for $200 a month. You have another demo next week with a similar trucking firm.
What do you build your pitch around?

options.text: The leading dispatch software: show you have more features for less money
options.feedback: This wins a contest the customer isn't running. They aren't choosing between two apps, so beating the rival on features doesn't move them.

options.text: The spreadsheet and phone calls they use now: show what that setup costs them each week
options.feedback: This speaks to the choice they're really making. You give up the easy feature comparison, but you finally argue against the thing that keeps winning.

options.text: Industry trends: show that firms who go digital grow faster
options.feedback: It may be true, but it's about firms in general. The owner is still asking why your app beats Rosa and her spreadsheet.

cards.title: The rival app was never in the room.
body: The founder had prepared slides comparing features with a bigger competitor. The owner had never looked at that competitor.
In his head, the choice was simple: pay $200 a month for something new, or keep a free system that mostly works. Rosa is fast. Problems get solved with a phone call.
Against that, a long feature list sounded like a cost, not a benefit.

cards.title: The customer's next best alternative
body: The **next best alternative** is what a customer would do if you didn't exist. It might be a rival, but often it's a workaround, a manual process, or simply putting up with the problem.

Your value is measured against that alternative, not against zero and not against the competitor you worry about. What matters is **how much better** you are than the customer's best other option, on the things they care about.

image.label: Two scales: your product versus the customer's current workaround
image.brief: 저울 인포그래픽. 한쪽 접시에 "Your product", 다른 쪽 접시에 "What they'd do without you"(스프레드시트, 전화, 손 작업 아이콘). 두 접시 사이의 높이 차이에 "Your real value" 라벨. 경쟁사 제품은 저울 밖 흐릿한 회색으로.

cards.title: "Free" is not the same as costless.
body: Against $0, a $200 app looks expensive. Against the hours Rosa spends rerouting trucks by phone, it can look cheap. The pitch should be built on this gap, and only if the time saved is real.

breakdown.label: Time saved per month
breakdown.detail: About 4 hours a week of rerouting calls

breakdown.label: Value of that time
breakdown.detail: At $30 an hour for the dispatcher

breakdown.label: What the customer gains
breakdown.detail: The gap over their next best alternative

cards.title: The alternative is rarely a product.
body: A custom cake competes with a supermarket cake, or with baking at home. A bookkeeper competes with the owner doing the books on Sunday night. A cleaning service competes with a teenager and a bucket.

Each alternative sets the bar you must clear. If the customer's workaround is cheap and good enough, your offer has to be clearly better on something they care about. If the workaround is painful, even a simple offer can win.

image.label: Each offer is judged against a homemade alternative.
image.brief: 세 칸 비교 일러스트. 1) 주문 케이크 옆에 마트 케이크와 집 오븐, 2) 회계 서비스 옆에 일요일 밤 식탁에서 영수증을 정리하는 사장님, 3) 청소 서비스 옆에 양동이를 든 청소년. 따뜻하고 친근한 톤, 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: Your math is not their math.
body: The hidden cost of a workaround is your story until the customer agrees with it. Many owners count their own or their staff's time as free. Ask them to estimate the cost, rather than telling them.

The alternative also changes by customer. One firm uses a spreadsheet, another has a nephew who built a tool. And even when you're clearly better, moving away from the old way has its own cost. That's the next lesson.

cards.title: Now it's a factory.
body: You make automatic pallet-wrapping machines. A mid-size food factory is interested. Today, two workers wrap pallets by hand with plastic film for part of each shift.

options.text: Compare your machine's speed and specs with a rival machine
options.feedback: Useful if they are already shopping for machines. But their real choice is machine versus hand-wrapping, so specs alone won't show why they should buy at all.

options.text: Compare against hand-wrapping: worker hours, film used and loads that arrive damaged
options.feedback: You argue against what they actually do today. It takes more homework on their numbers, but it turns the price into something they can weigh.

options.text: Offer a big discount so you're cheaper than the rival machine
options.feedback: You give away margin to beat a competitor they may not be considering. Hand-wrapping still looks free next to any price.

cards.title: You're compared with what they'd do without you.
body: Find the customer's next best alternative, then show how much better you are than that, in terms they recognise.
**Try it today:** ask one customer, "What did you do before you found us?" Write down their answer word for word. That's your real competitor.
